title: Lecture 00.90: Recent Advances (2022–2026) — Finite Data and the Shape of Point Clouds
content: Imagine walking into a dark room where someone has scattered a few hundred glowing grains of salt across an invisible doughnut. You can never touch the smooth surface itself—all you have is a finite list of 3D coordinates stored in a spreadsheet. Could you still prove, purely from those finite coordinates, that the hidden object has a hole through its center and a hollow cavity inside? That question turns the quietest chapter of point-set topology—sets, relations, and Euclidean distance—into one of the liveliest branches of modern data science: Topological Data Analysis TDA . Optional notes. Chapter 00 theory is not rewritten here. These notes show where sets, functions, and Euclidean space now live in 2022–2026 data science. The full theory track for this chapter is in Vietnamese; this English page holds recent-advance notes only. --- Key ideas: From Sets and Preorders to Topological Data Analysis A university graduate opening a topology textbook starts with abstract sets MATH , relations, and MATH , often wondering when any of this meets real data. Modern TDA bridges that gap across three pillars: 1. Finite Sets & Preorders as Alexandroff Topologies: On a finite set MATH , every topology corresponds one-to-one with a preorder a reflexive, transitive relation MATH , where the minimal open neighborhood of MATH is MATH . Thus finite relational tables and face posets of complexes are genuine topological spaces without ever needing a continuum! 2. Point Clouds to Simplicial Complexes Vietoris–Rips : Given a finite sample MATH and a scale radius MATH , we connect every pair with MATH by an edge, every mutually close triple by a filled triangle, and so on—building a nested filtration MATH as MATH grows. 3. Persistent Homology & Stability: Rather than guessing a single magic radius MATH , persistent homology tracks the birth and death radius of every connected component MATH , loop MATH , and void MATH across all scales, summarizing the dataset's shape as a barcode that is provably stable under small perturbations of the point cloud. --- 📖 Overview Chapter 00 starts every space from a set MATH and a family of subsets. In modern practice MATH is almost always finite: a point cloud MATH , a table, or a graph. The live question is no longer “is MATH complete?” but “from a finite set, how do we recover the shape of the continuum it samples?” That is the bridge from set theory to Topological Data Analysis TDA . The four advances below turn Chapter 00 language into algorithms. ! Point cloud on a torus https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4c/Point cloud torus.gif A torus sampled by finitely many points — the native object of TDA. Source: Wikimedia Commons https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Point cloud torus.gif --- 🎯 Intuition Imagine you never see the doughnut, only a handful of salt grains on its surface. You still “see” the hole if, after joining nearby grains by edges and triangles, that hole lives long enough as the joining radius grows. A finite set plus a nearness relation already talks about holes. Worked Example Step by Step : Vietoris–Rips Barcode of a 4-Point Square and a 3-Point Alexandroff Space Let's compute an entire persistent homology barcode by hand on just 4 points sitting at the corners of a unit square in MATH : MATH p 1 = 0,0 ,\quad p 2 = 1,0 ,\quad p 3 = 1,1 ,\quad p 4 = 0,1 . MATH Every side has Euclidean length MATH , and both diagonals have length MATH . Watch the Vietoris–Rips complex MATH evolve as radius MATH increases: | Scale interval MATH | Simplices present in MATH | Betti numbers MATH | Barcode events | |---|---|---|---| | MATH 0 \le r Definition reminder, not a new theory : a finite Alexandroff space has a minimal neighbourhood MATH at each point. A finite filtration is a nested sequence MATH X 0\subseteq X 1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq X m, MATH and persistent homology records classes MATH that still live in MATH . - Selçuk Kayacan, Persistent Homology via Finite Topological Spaces , arXiv:2512.23348 2025 . 2. TDA as the geometry of Euclidean samples Chazal–Michel remains the data-scientist’s doorway through 2022–2026: a datum is an element of a finite set, and “shape” is an invariant of complexes built from Euclidean distance. Su, Liu, Bou Hamdan, Maroulas, Wu, Carlsson, and Wei 2025 update the picture: TDA is now a family of invariants homotopy, sheaves, cell complexes grown from the same set-and-relation idea. - Frédéric Chazal, Bertrand Michel, An introduction to Topological Data Analysis: fundamental and practical aspects for data scientists , Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence 2021 , arXiv:1710.04019. - Zhe Su et al., Topological Data Analysis and Topological Deep Learning Beyond Persistent Homology — A Review , arXiv:2507.19504 2025 . 3. Gromov–Hausdorff stability for labeled sets Fu, Lagoda, Li, Needham, and Ver Hoef 2025 prove a Gromov–Hausdorff stability statement for persistent homology of labeled finite sets . If two finite metric samples are close as metric spaces, barcodes cannot jump far. “Set + map + Euclidean distance” becomes a stability theorem for machine learning. - Yaoying Fu, Evgeniya Lagoda, Shiying Li, Tom Needham, Lander Ver Hoef, Persistent Homology for Labeled Datasets: Gromov–Hausdorff Stability and Generalized Landscapes , arXiv:2512.08794 2025 . 4. Molecular TDA/TDL: data as a set of atoms Wee and Jiang 2025 survey how finite sets of atoms — sets, not smooth manifolds — become topological features for chemical AI. Chapter 00 is enough to start reading those papers. - JunJie Wee, Jian Jiang, A review of topological data analysis and topological deep learning in molecular sciences , arXiv:2509.16877 2025 . --- 🧠 Papers and references - James R. Munkres, Topology , 2nd ed., Ch. 1. - Sidney A. Morris, Topology without Tears , Ch. 1–2. - The arXiv items above 2021–2025 . 🔗 Applications In cheminformatics a molecule is a finite set of atoms with a bonding relation. Persistent homology reads its holes across scales — the same set/function language as Lectures 00.00–00.03. title: Lecture 01.90: Recent Advances (2022–2026) — Topology of Data and Clustering
content: Every data scientist has had the same unsettling experience: you run a clustering algorithm on a biological dataset, tweak one neighborhood parameter by 10%, and suddenly two tidy cell populations shatter into five fragments—or fuse into one blob. Beneath that practical headache hides the very first definition of general topology: what counts as an open neighborhood, and when does a map preserve nearness without tearing space apart? Optional notes. Open sets, bases, closure, and continuity in Chapter 01 stay as they are. These notes show how they reappear when MATH is a point cloud in 2022–2026 research. The theory track is in Vietnamese; this English page holds recent-advance notes only. --- Key ideas: How Open Sets, Continuity, and Superlevel Sets Power Modern Clustering To a university graduate, the axioms of a topological space can feel oddly detached from data algorithms. In 2022–2026 machine learning, three Chapter 01 concepts sit right inside the engine: 1. Coarser vs. Finer Topologies as Scale Knobs: Choosing a smaller neighborhood radius MATH or fewer MATH -nearest neighbors creates a finer topology with many small open pieces; enlarging MATH passes to a coarser topology that glues pieces together. Comparing topologies across all scales at once is the core of persistent clustering . 2. Density Superlevel Sets & Mode Prominence ToMATo : Given an estimated data density MATH , the superlevel sets MATH form an expanding family of open sets as threshold MATH drops from MATH to MATH . Each density peak births a cluster, and each saddle point merges two clusters—measuring each cluster's true prominence rather than relying on one brittle cutoff. 3. Continuity vs. Homeomorphism in Dimension Reduction: A continuous map MATH guarantees that preimages of open sets are open—meaning nearby points stay nearby, though distinct clusters can still collide. Only a homeomorphism preserves topology both ways. Popular projections like UMAP approximate local neighborhoods, so dropping a single bridge edge in the neighbor graph can tear one cluster into two! --- 📖 Overview A topology on MATH is a way to say which points sit next to which, without a metric. Clustering is the same question written as an algorithm: which pieces of the data are natural “open chunks”? From 2022 to 2026, topological clustering left the appendix of TDA books and became multiscale, multiparameter, and stable. ! Clustering https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c8/Cluster-2.svg Two planar clusters: a discrete picture of disconnectedness. Source: Wikimedia Commons https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Cluster-2.svg --- 🎯 Intuition Recall an open set: if MATH , a whole “region around MATH ” stays in MATH . In data that region is usually MATH neighbours or an MATH -ball. Small MATH makes every point a cluster; large MATH glues everything. Persistent clustering watches clusters through MATH — the same spirit as comparing coarser/finer topologies in Lecture 01.01. Worked Example Step by Step : Tracking Superlevel-Set Clusters and Prominence on a 5-Point Density Profile Suppose we sample a 1D dataset along a path of 5 adjacent points MATH whose estimated density values are: MATH \rho x 1 = 5,\quad \rho x 2 = 2,\quad \rho x 3 = 1,\quad \rho x 4 = 4,\quad \rho x 5 = 2. MATH There are two clear density peaks—at MATH height 5 and MATH height 4 —separated by a valley at MATH height 1 . Sweep the threshold MATH downward and record the connected components of the open superlevel set MATH : | Threshold MATH | Superlevel set MATH | Connected components | Topological event | |---|---|---|---| | MATH | MATH | 1 | Cluster A born at height MATH | | MATH | MATH | 2 | Cluster B born at height MATH | | MATH | MATH | 2 | Both clusters grow; valley MATH still separates them | | MATH | MATH | 1 | Valley MATH enters → B merges into A at height MATH | By the Elder Rule the higher peak survives, the younger peak dies at the saddle , Cluster B has persistence prominence MATH , while Cluster A persists forever MATH . Now imagine a noisy bump of height MATH sitting next to the valley: its prominence is only MATH . Choosing a prominence cutoff MATH cleanly keeps the 2 real clusters and discards the noise bump—something no single fixed density threshold MATH could achieve if one true cluster were slightly shorter than another! Explanation: Why Topological Clustering Beats Single-Threshold Clustering 1. Replace one fragile threshold with a full filtration: single-threshold density clustering like classic DBSCAN with one fixed density fails when Cluster A has peak density 5 and Cluster B has peak density 2 while a valley sits at 1; sweeping MATH sees every peak at its own native scale. 2. Measure cluster significance by lifetime prominence : a cluster's persistence MATH is literally the depth of the valley separating it from a taller neighbor—a coordinate-free topological invariant of the density function. 3. Move to multiparameter filtrations when density and scale interact: real datasets vary in both local density MATH and geometric radius MATH ; 2025–2026 methods like ToMAToMP track components across both parameters simultaneously to resist outliers. 4. Audit dimension-reduction plots with continuity: before trusting two separated blobs on a UMAP scatter plot, remember that UMAP is not guaranteed to be a homeomorphism—check whether the separation already lives in the high-dimensional MATH persistence diagram! Quick check. In our 5-point example, what happens to the persistence prominence of Cluster B if the valley MATH rises from MATH to MATH ? Its prominence shrinks from MATH down to MATH , immediately signaling that the two peaks have nearly merged into a single broad cluster. --- 📐 Four concrete advances 1. Persistent multiscale density-based clustering Bot, McInnes, and Aerts 2025 introduce Persistent Multiscale Density-based Clustering : instead of one density threshold they track connected components of density superlevel sets as a filtration. Chapter 01 becomes an algorithm: the open sets MATH move with MATH , and the topology changes under control. - Daniël Bot, Leland McInnes, Jan Aerts, Persistent Multiscale Density-based Clustering , arXiv:2512.16558 2025 . 2. ToMATo again: multiparameter topological clustering The ToMATo line Topological Mode Analysis Tool pairs density modes with MATH -dimensional persistence. Martineau, Pouzat, and Geffray 2025 take ToMATo to high-dimensional spike sorting. Andrianirina and Carrière 2026 extend it to ToMAToMP — stable multiparameter clustering. A “mode” is a peak of a density; a “valley” is where clusters meet — a very point-set picture of closure and boundary. - Louise Martineau, Christophe Pouzat, Ségolen Geffray, ToMATo: an efficient and robust clustering algorithm for high dimensional datasets , arXiv:2509.17499 2025 . - Ludo Andrianirina, Mathieu Carrière, ToMAToMP: Robust and Multi-Parameter Topological Clustering , arXiv:2605.14824 2026 . 3. Continuity and homeomorphism in dimension reduction UMAP claims to preserve local topology. Dalmia and Sia 2021; still shaping 2022–2026 practice show that connectivity of the neighbour graph decides cluster quality after UMAP: lose an edge and you lose a component. That is Lecture 01.03 in experimental form: a merely “almost continuous” map can break a homeomorphism type and merge or split clusters. - Ayush Dalmia, Suzanna Sia, Clustering with UMAP: Why and How Connectivity Matters , arXiv:2108.05525 2021 . 4. Neural networks as topological spaces of data Ballester, Casacuberta, and Escalera 2023/24 survey TDA on neural networks: weights, activations, and datasets are treated as spaces. The forward pass is a map in the sense of Chapter 01, except MATH has millions of points. - Rubén Ballester, Carles Casacuberta, Sergio Escalera, Topological Data Analysis for Neural Network Analysis: A Comprehensive Survey , arXiv:2312.05840 2023 . Formal reminder: if MATH is continuous and MATH is open, then MATH is open. In an encoder, “open” is usually an ambient ball in latent space. When the encoder fails this, clusters tear. --- 🧠 Papers and references - Munkres, Topology , Ch. 2. - Adams & Franzosa, Introduction to Topology: Pure and Applied , Ch. 1. - The arXiv items above. 🔗 Applications Single-cell grouping uses UMAP plus density clustering. These notes let you read the 2025–2026 papers without leaving Chapter 01. This note then explains why that is not yet a homeomorphism. - Henry Adams 5/3/22 : Topology in Machine Learning https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kwYiQNa pTc — Applied Algebraic Topology Network, English. Topology used as a feature of data and of clustering, close to the TDA items here. - An introduction to persistent homology https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UxEH7WySO60 — Applied Algebraic Topology Network, English. Components and holes across scales, which is what a clustering algorithm is trying to see. 🧩 Exercises 1. Draw two topologies on the same 5 points: one with 2 clusters, one with 1. Which is finer? 2. Why does increasing MATH in MATH -NN look like passing to a coarser topology? 3. Take a density on MATH with two peaks. Sketch the filtration MATH as MATH drops.

title: Lecture 02.90: Recent Advances (2022–2026) — Connectedness, Compactness, and Components of Data
content: Train the exact same neural network twice from two different random seeds, and you land at two completely different weight vectors MATH and MATH in billion-dimensional space—yet both achieve 95% accuracy. For years, researchers pictured those minima as isolated mountain valleys separated by steep walls of high loss. Then came a topological surprise: in many deep networks, you can walk along a continuous, low-loss valley all the way from MATH to MATH without ever climbing a hill—and sometimes even along a straight line segment! That phenomenon, mode connectivity , is nothing other than path-connectedness of sublevel sets in action. Optional notes. Connectedness, path-connectedness, and compactness stay as in Chapter 02. We follow them into data and neural parameter space across 2022–2026 research. The theory track is in Vietnamese; this English page holds recent-advance notes only. --- Key ideas: Connectedness, Compactness, and Modern Loss Landscapes Two cornerstone properties from Chapter 02— connectedness and compactness —govern how modern AI practitioners cluster data, merge models, and stabilize topological features: 1. Connectedness & Path-Connectedness: A space is connected if it cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open sets, and path-connected if any two points can be joined by a continuous curve MATH . In TDA, MATH persistence tracks path-components of data across scales; in deep learning, mode connectivity asks whether the low-loss sublevel set MATH is path-connected. 2. Linear Mode Connectivity & Model Merging: Stronger than arbitrary path-connectedness is convexity along the chord : does the straight segment MATH stay inside MATH ? When it does, averaging the weights of two separately fine-tuned LLMs model merging preserves accuracy without paying for an ensemble! 3. Compactness as Stability Control: In MATH , Heine–Borel characterizes compactness as closed and bounded—forcing every continuous function to attain its bounds and every open cover to reduce to a finite subcover. In TDA, compactness guarantees finite-like control over persistence diagrams so that stable vectorizations Lipschitz maps into Banach/Euclidean spaces never blow up under tiny perturbations. --- 📖 Overview The two “most important” point-set properties — cannot be split and every open cover has a finite subcover — are the language of two modern questions: 1 how many pieces does the data have? 2 can a family of models walk from one minimum to another without climbing a loss wall? ! Source: Wikimedia Commons https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mug and Torus morph.gif --- 🎯 Intuition A connected space cannot be written MATH with MATH open, nonempty, and disjoint. In clustering that is the definition of “one cluster” at a fixed scale. MATH persistence refines it: two points lie in the same component at radius MATH when a chain of intermediate points has steps of length MATH . Compactness appears when we ask whether barcodes are stable: the space of persistence diagrams bottleneck metric is complete, and finite diagrams behave in a Heine–Borel “finite-like” way. title: Lecture 03.90: Recent Advances (2022–2026) — Separation, Embeddings, and Stable Shape
content: Open almost any genomics or AI paper today and you will see a colorful 2D scatter plot produced by UMAP, accompanied by the triumphant caption "the embedding cleanly separates the two patient groups." Yet a point-set topologist pauses immediately: can you actually embed that high-dimensional structure into MATH without tearing or gluing points together, or is the plot merely a spectral-clustering illusion? Answering that question brings Chapter 03's classic separation axioms MATH and metrization theorems straight into the heart of 2022–2026 machine learning. Optional notes. The axioms MATH – MATH , Urysohn’s lemma, and metrization stay as in Chapter 03. We ask in what sense data and TDA invariants truly “separate points.” The theory track is in Vietnamese; this English page holds recent-advance notes only. --- Key ideas: Separation Axioms, Topological Embeddings, and Stable Barcodes Why do mathematicians bother distinguishing MATH , MATH , MATH Hausdorff , and MATH normal spaces? Three pillars show how this hierarchy bites in modern TDA and representation learning: 1. The Separation Hierarchy MATH : In a MATH space, distinct points merely have some open set containing one without the other true of finite Alexandroff spaces used inside TDA pipelines . In a Hausdorff MATH space, distinct points enjoy disjoint open neighborhoods—guaranteeing unique limits and making distance-based reasoning coherent. Every metric space is automatically MATH even MATH . 2. Topological Embeddings vs. Visual Projections: A map MATH is a true topological embedding only if it is a homeomorphism onto its image MATH . Projecting a 2-sphere MATH or a high-dimensional manifold into MATH cannot be an embedding without cutting or collapsing points—so 2D UMAP plots routinely distort global distances and invent false separations. 3. Metrization & Lipschitz Stability: Equipping persistence diagrams with the bottleneck metric MATH turns diagram space into a Hausdorff metric space. Modern vectorization theory goes one step beyond Urysohn's continuous separating functions by demanding Lipschitz maps so tiny data noise cannot explode downstream ML features. --- 📖 Overview Hausdorff means distinct points have disjoint neighbourhoods — limits, when they exist, are unique. Machine learning often assumes this when it draws a UMAP: distinct points should sit in two places. Work from 2022–2026 shows the assumption is both necessary barcode stability and fragile UMAP is not a topological embedding . ! Hausdorff distance https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/21/Hausdorff distance sample.svg Hausdorff distance between two sets: the MATH idea, metrized. Source: Wikimedia Commons https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hausdorff distance sample.svg --- 🎯 Intuition Urysohn’s lemma says that in a sufficiently nice normal space, disjoint closed sets are separated by a continuous MATH -valued function. Mapper and UMAP try to draw that function for data. When the space is not Hausdorff — e.g. Kayacan’s finite Alexandroff spaces Lecture 00.90 — point-separation fails and embedding algorithms start inventing distances. Worked Example Step by Step : A Non-Hausdorff MATH Space and an Exact Bottleneck Distance MATH Verify both sides of Chapter 03—failure of MATH on finite spaces, and success of MATH on persistence diagrams—by hand: Part A — Sierpiński space MATH , yet fails MATH and MATH . Let MATH with open sets MATH . - Check MATH : for MATH , the open set MATH contains MATH and excludes MATH → MATH holds! - Check Hausdorff MATH : the only open set containing MATH is MATH , which necessarily overlaps MATH . No disjoint open neighborhoods exist → not MATH ! - Consequence for limits: the constant sequence MATH eventually lies inside every open set containing MATH namely MATH , so it converges to both MATH and MATH simultaneously! Part B — Exact bottleneck distance MATH between two persistence diagrams. Suppose Diagram MATH has one real loop MATH lifetime MATH , while noisy Diagram MATH has a slightly perturbed loop MATH plus a small spurious noise loop MATH . In the bottleneck metric, points are matched bijectively allowing unmatched points to pair with the diagonal MATH to minimize the largest MATH shift: - Pair MATH with MATH : cost MATH . - Pair the noise point MATH with its closest diagonal point MATH : cost MATH . - Therefore: MATH d B D 1, D 2 = \max 0.3,\ 0.2 = \mathbf 0.3 . MATH Because MATH is a metric, distinct diagrams sit inside disjoint open MATH -balls MATH ! , and tiny noise loops near the diagonal only nudge MATH by half their lifetime. Explanation: Why Separation Axioms Decide When Embeddings and Barcodes Are Trustworthy 1. Finite TDA pipelines naturally live in non-Hausdorff MATH spaces: every finite simplicial complex's face poset is a MATH Alexandroff space like a larger Sierpiński space ; non-Hausdorff topology is not a pathology—it is the native combinatorial engine! 2. Passing to homology lands in a Hausdorff metric space: once persistent homology extracts a diagram and equips it with MATH , distinct shapes become cleanly separated by disjoint open balls, making limits and stability theorems well-defined. 3. Never equate "drawn in MATH " with "topological embedding": as Yang 2026 proves, UMAP behaves like spectral clustering on a fuzzy neighbor graph—visually splitting or merging regions that were not separated in the original space. 4. Upgrade continuity to Lipschitz stability for ML: Urysohn's lemma promises continuous separating functions, yet machine learning requires Lipschitz vectorizations so small noise MATH in data produces at most MATH change in features. Quick check. In Part B, if a second noise point MATH appeared in MATH , what would MATH become? Its distance to the diagonal is MATH , so MATH rises to MATH —strictly controlled by the single worst perturbation. --- 📐 Four concrete advances 1. Diagram space is Hausdorff — that is why stability means anything The bottleneck metric MATH on persistence diagrams satisfies MATH d B \mathrm Dgm X ,\mathrm Dgm Y \le d GH X,Y MATH under compact hypotheses. MATH is metric, hence MATH : distinct barcodes are ball-separated. Now flip that same gluing idea onto a noisy dataset of 50,000 breast-cancer gene profiles: slice the dataset into overlapping strips by a summary function, cluster each strip, and glue overlapping clusters by edges. By the Nerve Theorem, when the cover is fine enough, this graph recovers the homotopy type of MATH a discrete Reeb graph! . 3. title: Lecture 08.90: Recent Advances (2022–2026) — Topological Deep Learning and Computational Morse
content: Graph Neural Networks GNNs conquered social networks and basic chemistry by passing messages along pairwise edges. Yet look closely at a benzene ring, a protein folding pocket, or three scientists co-authoring a single paper: a three-way interaction is fundamentally different from three separate pairwise conversations! Between 2022 and 2026, Topological Deep Learning TDL broke past the pairwise graph barrier by letting neural networks pass messages across triangles, polygons, and higher-dimensional cells—while Discrete Morse Theory quietly became the high-speed preprocessor powering topological computation at scale. Optional notes. Higher homotopy, fiber bundles, Morse theory, manifolds, and knots stay as in Chapter 08. We watch them become learning architectures and reduction algorithms . The theory track is in Vietnamese; this English page holds recent-advance notes only. --- Key ideas: Higher-Order Complexes, Hodge Laplacians, and Discrete Morse Theory Three advanced topological pillars from Chapter 08 now sit directly inside modern geometric AI and computational topology: 1. Beyond Graphs — Simplicial & Cell Complexes: A graph only stores 0-cells vertices and 1-cells edges . A simplicial complex adds 2-cells filled triangles , 3-cells tetrahedra , and higher faces; a cell complex allows arbitrary rings like 6-carbon benzene hexagons as single 2-cells—giving molecular and relational AI native higher-order inductive bias. 2. Hodge Laplacians & Higher-Order Message Passing TDL : On a graph, messages diffuse via the graph Laplacian MATH . On a simplicial complex, signals living on edges such as traffic flows or chemical bond currents diffuse via the 1-Hodge Laplacian MATH , combining lower adjacency through shared vertices and upper adjacency through shared triangles ! 3. Discrete Morse Theory Robin Forman : Just as smooth Morse theory reconstructs a manifold from its critical points minima, saddles, maxima , discrete Morse theory pairs non-critical MATH -cells with MATH -cells to collapse away redundant simplices while preserving exact homotopy type—slashing huge complexes down to a tiny skeleton of critical cells . --- 📖 Overview Topological deep learning TDL trains models on data supported by simplicial complexes, cell complexes, and hypergraphs — the domains Chapter 08 just named. Hajij et al. 2022/23 set the foundation; Papillon et al. 2023/24 classify message-passing architectures; Papamarkou et al. ICML 2024 position call TDL the frontier of relational learning. In parallel, discrete Morse theory became the reduction engine for persistence on huge data. ! A simplicial network talks along triangles: three nodes already “know” they span a MATH -face. That is Morse and CW from Lectures 08.02–08.03 written as a layer. Fiber bundles appear when features live on fibres that twist around the base — the gauge language of physics, now a trainable layer. Explanation: From Higher-Order Complexes to TDL and Morse Reductions 1. Match the domain to the physics: when data carries genuine multi-body interactions protein pockets, aromatic rings, co-authorship cliques , lifting a graph to a simplicial or cell complex lets a single message-passing step aggregate the entire group at once. 2. Use Hodge decomposition to separate signal types: MATH splits any edge signal cleanly into gradient flows from vertices , curl flows around triangles , and harmonic flows around true holes —giving TDL layers crisp spectral structure. 3. Collapse before you compute Discrete Morse : by pairing adjacent MATH -cells into acyclic arrows, Morse reductions delete millions of trivial cells from 3D grids while keeping every topological feature critical cell intact. 4. title: Lecture 09.90: Recent Advances (2022–2026) — Materials, Neuroscience, Graphs, and Popular TDA
content: In 1736, Leonhard Euler stood over a map of Königsberg's seven bridges and realized that geography didn't matter—only how vertices and edges connect. Fourteen years later, he wrote down MATH for convex polyhedra. Nearly three centuries on, those very same ideas are no longer charming puzzle-book anecdotes: in 2022–2026 laboratories, direction-aware Euler characteristic curves predict the elastic stiffness of porous metamaterials, persistent MATH loops decode scale-invariant rhythms in human brain connectomes, and Mapper graphs chart semantic neighborhoods across entire corpora of language and video games! Optional notes. The coffee–doughnut, Königsberg, Möbius, Euler, four-colour, DNA, physics, and Poincaré stories stay as they are. We add where they now run in applied 2022–2026 papers. The theory / popular-science track is in Vietnamese; this English page holds recent-advance notes only. --- Key ideas: From Euler's Formula to Materials, Brain Networks, and NLP How do Chapter 09's classic visual stories translate into quantitative lab measurements? Three mathematical bridges do the heavy lifting: 1. Euler Characteristic MATH : The single most portable topological invariant in science—computed simply by counting vertices, edges, and faces, yet guaranteed to equal the alternating sum of Betti numbers components minus loops plus cavities ! 2. Direction-Aware Topological Descriptors Euler Characteristic Transform : A static Betti number forgets which way a pore or fiber points. Sweeping a plane across a 3D porous material along every unit direction MATH and recording the curve MATH captures both topology and anisotropic geometry—enough to predict full mechanical stiffness tensors Topolnicki et al., 2026 ! 3. Cycle Space MATH in Connectomes and Language Graphs: For any connected graph no 2-faces , Euler's formula simplifies to MATH —counting independent feedback loops. Tracking how MATH and MATH evolve as edge-weight thresholds sweep across a brain network or word co-occurrence graph reveals higher-order structure invisible to simple node-degree counts. --- 📖 Overview Chapter 09 teaches topology by pictures. Groups in 2022–2026 do the symmetric thing: take those pictures — holes, knots, networks, surfaces — and measure them on porous materials, biological neural nets, social graphs, and language. This page is a reading map, not a new physics or biology lecture. ! Persistent homology counts the holes of a graph or an atomic cloud across scales . No new formula is required: a filtration is. That is why Chapter 09 and Chapter 07 meet in the lab. Same vertex count, same edge count, yet different global topology—immediately visible to MATH . Explanation: How Euler's 1750 Formula Became a 2026 Scientific Instrument 1. Start with a single invariant number MATH : counting vertices, edges, and faces is blazingly fast— MATH —and invariant under any subdivision or rubber-sheet deformation. 2. Add a filtration to turn a number into a curve: sweeping a scale threshold correlation strength in a connectome, or height MATH in a 3D porous scan transforms MATH into an Euler Characteristic Curve that tracks when pores open and close. 3. Sweep over directions to recover anisotropic physics: a porous foam with vertical tunnels is stiffer vertically than horizontally; direction-aware topological descriptors record MATH curves along dozens of angles to predict directional stiffness tensors. 4. Move from passive features to trainable architectures: once topological summaries prove predictive in materials, neuroscience, and NLP, Topological Deep Learning TDL bakes those exact complexes directly into neural network layers.
